--- title: "Linear and polynomial regression" description: "Linear regression is the yardstick every method in this section must beat. One squared input lets it find the temperature a species prefers, but nothing in it knows that a count stops at zero." order: 1 categories: [supervised, regression] --- {{< new-terms >}} ## Every method must beat linear regression on new sites Linear regression is the simplest model for a quantity, and the yardstick for every method in this section: each is scored on the same new sites, and a more complex method earns its place only by beating it. One small change, a squared input, lets the straight line bend and find the temperature a species prefers. What neither the line nor the curve can learn is that a count stops at zero. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## A squared input bends the line into a curve A linear regression adds a starting value to a fixed amount for each input, the input's coefficient times its value ([Prediction and explanation](../01-introduction/prediction-and-explanation.qmd#linear-regression-gives-one-slope-per-input)). One extra unit of an input changes the prediction by the same amount wherever you start, so the prediction is a straight line in each input. A straight line cannot rise and then fall. Adding the square of an input as one more column lets it: $$\hat{y} = a + b x + c x^2$$ This is **polynomial regression**, and it is still linear regression. The prediction is still a starting value plus a coefficient times each column; one of the columns happens to be a square. "Linear" refers to how the coefficients combine, not to the shape of the curve. When $c$ is negative the curve has one peak, at $x = -b / 2c$. That is the shape of an optimum: a species that does best at one temperature or depth and less well on either side. ::: {.diagram} ![A straight line has one slope. Adding a squared input bends it into a curve with one peak, still fitted by linear regression. Beyond the data, the curve keeps going, even below zero.](img/line-to-curve.svg){fig-alt="Three cards. Straight line: a plus b times the input; each extra unit of the input adds the same amount, wherever you start. Curve: a plus b times the input plus c times the input squared; the curve rises to a peak, marked optimum, and falls again; it is still linear regression, a weighted sum of columns, one of them a square. Beyond the data: a shaded band marks the range of the data, the curve peaks inside it and, dashed, keeps falling outside it on both sides, below a line marking zero. A note says a curve can follow a peak that a straight line misses, but only inside the range of the data."} ::: Outside the range of the data, a curve keeps rising or falling, and nothing in the model checks where it goes; [Uneven sampling and extrapolation](../06-assumptions-limitations/sampling-and-extrapolation.qmd) deals with predicting there. ## Worked example The outcome is the survey's count of one species, with depth, temperature, chlorophyll, salinity, seabed type and season as inputs. A quarter of the sites are held back as test sites, as [Splitting the data](../02-marine-data/splitting-data.qmd) recommends, so the models are scored on sites they have never seen. The two recipes differ in one step: `step_poly()` adds the squares of depth and temperature, and `raw = TRUE` keeps them as plain squares, so the coefficients mean what they do in the equation above. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() split <- group_initial_split(survey, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) train <- training(split) test <- testing(split) predictors <- abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate + season line_recipe <- recipe(predictors, data = train) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |> step_relevel(substrate, ref_level = "sand") curve_recipe <- line_recipe |> step_poly(depth_m, temperature_c, degree = 2, options = list(raw = TRUE)) ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, PolynomialFeatures from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() numeric = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"] categorical = ["substrate", "season"] predictors = numeric + categorical grouper = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) train_rows, test_rows = next(grouper.split(survey, groups=survey["site_id"])) train, test = survey.iloc[train_rows], survey.iloc[test_rows] # The dropped level of each column is its baseline: sand, and spring as in R. dummies = OneHotEncoder(drop=["sand", "spring"], sparse_output=False) line_recipe = ColumnTransformer([ ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), numeric), ("categorical", dummies, categorical), ]) # One PolynomialFeatures per column, as step_poly() does: given both columns # at once, it would also add depth times temperature. def squared(column): return (column, Pipeline([ ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("poly", PolynomialFeatures(degree=2, include_bias=False)), ]), [column]) curve_recipe = ColumnTransformer([ squared("depth_m"), squared("temperature_c"), ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), ["chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"]), ("categorical", dummies, categorical), ]) ``` ::: ::: ### Polynomial regression finds a peak linear regression misses Both models are fitted on the training sites. The table shows the coefficients for depth and temperature; in R, `_poly_1` is the input and `_poly_2` its square. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} line_fit <- workflow(line_recipe, linear_reg()) |> fit(train) curve_fit <- workflow(curve_recipe, linear_reg()) |> fit(train) bind_rows( tidy(line_fit) |> mutate(model = "Linear regression"), tidy(curve_fit) |> mutate(model = "Polynomial regression") ) |> filter(str_detect(term, "depth|temperature")) |> transmute(model, term, estimate = as.character(signif(estimate, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|model |term |estimate | |:---------------------|:--------------------|:--------| |Linear regression |depth_m |-0.0322 | |Linear regression |temperature_c |-0.328 | |Polynomial regression |depth_m_poly_1 |-0.0535 | |Polynomial regression |depth_m_poly_2 |0.000111 | |Polynomial regression |temperature_c_poly_1 |2.27 | |Polynomial regression |temperature_c_poly_2 |-0.151 |
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression def fit(recipe): return Pipeline([("recipe", recipe), ("model", LinearRegression())]).fit( train[predictors], train["abundance"]) def coefficients(fitted, label): table = pd.DataFrame({"model": label, "term": fitted[:-1].get_feature_names_out(), "estimate": fitted[-1].coef_}) table = table[table["term"].str.contains("depth|temperature")] return table.assign(estimate=table["estimate"].map(lambda v: float(f"{v:.3g}"))) line_fit = fit(line_recipe) curve_fit = fit(curve_recipe) pd.concat([coefficients(line_fit, "Linear regression"), coefficients(curve_fit, "Polynomial regression")], ignore_index=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | model | term | estimate | |:----------------------|:-------------------------------|-----------:| | Linear regression | numeric__depth_m | -0.044 | | Linear regression | numeric__temperature_c | -0.728 | | Polynomial regression | depth_m__depth_m | -0.0548 | | Polynomial regression | depth_m__depth_m^2 | 7.76e-05 | | Polynomial regression | temperature_c__temperature_c | 1.6 | | Polynomial regression | temperature_c__temperature_c^2 | -0.129 | ::: ::: ::: The straight line gives temperature one coefficient, −0.33: each extra degree lowers the predicted count by 0.33 animals, in the coldest water and the warmest alike. For the curve, $b$ is 2.27 and $c$ is −0.151. $c$ is negative, so the curve has a peak, at $-b / 2c$ = 7.5 °C, well inside the survey's 1.9 to 16 °C. Fitted through a hump, a straight line averages the rising side with the falling side, and its one slope describes neither: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} grid <- tibble( temperature_c = seq(temp_range[1], temp_range[2], length.out = 200), depth_m = median(train$depth_m, na.rm = TRUE), chlorophyll_mg_m3 = median(train$chlorophyll_mg_m3, na.rm = TRUE), salinity_psu = median(train$salinity_psu, na.rm = TRUE), substrate = factor("sand", levels = levels(train$substrate)), season = factor("summer", levels = levels(train$season)) ) curves <- bind_rows( augment(line_fit, grid) |> mutate(model = "Linear regression"), augment(curve_fit, grid) |> mutate(model = "Polynomial regression") ) ggplot(curves, aes(temperature_c, .pred, colour = model)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = ml_palette[["grey"]], linewidth = 0.6) + geom_rug(data = train, aes(temperature_c), inherit.aes = FALSE, sides = "b", alpha = 0.3, colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) + scale_colour_manual(values = c("Linear regression" = ml_palette[["blue"]], "Polynomial regression" = ml_palette[["orange"]]), breaks = c("Linear regression", "Polynomial regression")) + labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Predicted count", colour = NULL, title = "Polynomial regression finds a peak the straight line misses") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The predicted count across the survey's temperatures, with the other inputs held at their typical values (sand, summer, median depth, chlorophyll and salinity). The ticks along the bottom are the training stations. Linear regression falls steadily; polynomial regression finds the peak and falls below zero in warm water.](linear-and-polynomial-regression_files/figure-html/fig-shapes-1.png){#fig-shapes fig-alt='Two lines of predicted count against temperature, with a horizontal line marking zero and ticks along the bottom showing the temperatures of the training stations. The linear regression line declines slowly. The polynomial regression curve rises from the cold end to a peak in the middle of the range, then falls steeply and crosses zero before the warm end of the data.' width=1500} ::: ::: ::: ### Polynomial regression scores better but predicts fewer than zero animals Both models are scored on the test sites with the [RMSE](../01-introduction/prediction-and-explanation.qmd#rmse-measures-a-typical-miss-on-the-test-stations), the typical miss in animals, and [$R^2$](../02-marine-data/information-leakage.qmd#one-linear-regression-shows-each-kind), the share of the variation in the test counts that the predictions follow. The last two columns give the lowest prediction and the number of predictions below zero. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} score <- function(fitted, label) { predictions <- augment(fitted, test) tibble( model = label, rmse = rmse_vec(predictions$abundance, predictions$.pred), rsq = rsq_trad_vec(predictions$abundance, predictions$.pred), lowest = min(predictions$.pred), below_zero = sum(predictions$.pred < 0) ) } scores <- bind_rows( score(line_fit, "Linear regression"), score(curve_fit, "Polynomial regression") ) scores |> mutate(across(rmse:lowest, \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|model | rmse| rsq| lowest| below_zero| |:---------------------|----:|----:|------:|----------:| |Linear regression | 3.75| 0.14| -0.40| 1| |Polynomial regression | 3.62| 0.19| -3.86| 12|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} from sklearn.metrics import r2_score, root_mean_squared_error def score(fitted, label): predicted = fitted.predict(test[predictors]) truth = test["abundance"] return { "model": label, "rmse": round(root_mean_squared_error(truth, predicted), 2), "rsq": round(r2_score(truth, predicted), 2), "lowest": round(predicted.min(), 2), "below_zero": int((predicted < 0).sum()), } pd.DataFrame([score(line_fit, "Linear regression"), score(curve_fit, "Polynomial regression")]) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | model | rmse | rsq | lowest | below_zero | |:----------------------|-------:|------:|---------:|-------------:| | Linear regression | 4.9 | 0.21 | -1.88 | 1 | | Polynomial regression | 4.73 | 0.26 | -1.45 | 10 | ::: ::: ::: On sites the models have never seen, the curve does better: $R^2$ rises from 0.14 to 0.19, and the RMSE falls from 3.75 to 3.62 animals. The better model is also the more impossible one. The curve predicts a negative count at 12 of the 202 test stations, the lowest −3.9 animals; the line does so at 1. Nothing in linear regression knows that a count stops at zero, and the curve falls steeply after its peak, so it crosses zero sooner. Setting the negative predictions to zero hides the symptom, not the cause. [Regression for counts](count-regression.qmd) uses a model whose predictions cannot go below zero. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - Linear regression is the yardstick: every method in this section is scored against it on the same new sites. - Adding a squared input bends the line into a curve with one peak. It is still linear regression, and it suits a species with a preferred temperature or depth. - On the survey, the line gives temperature one slope, −0.33 animals per degree, while the curve finds a peak at 7.5 °C and scores better on new sites. - Neither knows that a count stops at zero: the curve predicts a negative count at 12 of 202 test stations. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Change `degree = 2` to `degree = 3` in `curve_recipe`. Does the test RMSE improve, and what happens to the temperature curve at the cold and warm ends? 2. Draw the grid from 0 to 25 °C instead of the survey's range, and redraw the figure. Where does each model go outside the data?
